iyi (good) plus -yim (I am). The usual answer to nasılsın?
To one friend. Politely or to a group: ya siz?
Said by the one who leaves, to one friend. The one who stays answers güle güle.
To one friend. Politely or to a group: kendinize iyi bakın.
nere (where) + -li (from) + -sin (you are). Politely: nerelisiniz?
A fixed phrase for a first meeting, literally 'I became pleased'.
Kardeş alone means a brother or a sister. An older brother is often called abi.
Kardeş alone means a brother or a sister. An older sister is often called abla.
Many people say anneanne (mother's mother) or babaanne (father's mother).

Nice and caring to people. It also means polite.
For people only. An old thing, like an old house, is eski.

To one friend. Politely: kaç yaşındasınız?

body.en:
Turkish has no separate word for 'am' or 'are'. Instead you add a short ending to the word: öğrenci (student) becomes öğrenciyim (I am a student), and öğretmen (teacher) becomes öğretmensin (you are a teacher). For 'he' or 'she' you add nothing: O mutlu means 'he or she is happy'.

The vowel in the ending follows the last vowel of the word: i after e or i, ı after a or ı, u after o or u, ü after ö or ü. This is vowel harmony, and you will meet it everywhere: iyiyim, nasılsın, yorgunum, Türküm. Watch the dots too: ı and i are two different letters. After a vowel, a y slips in: iyi + im = iyiyim.

Because the ending already says who, ben (I) and sen (you) are often left out: İyiyim alone means 'I am fine'. The word with 'am', 'are' or 'is' goes last, and bir (a) comes after a describing word: Anna Berlinli bir öğretmen, Anna is a teacher from Berlin.

examples.en: I am a student.
You are very kind.
I am fine, and you?

title.en: My, your, his: endings that say whose

body.en:
To say whose something is, Turkish puts an ending on the thing itself. After a vowel: annem (my mother), annen (your mother), annesi (his or her mother). After a consonant, a vowel comes first: kardeşim, kardeşin, kardeşi. For 'our', add -miz or -imiz: köpeğimiz (our dog).

The vowel follows harmony again: babam, evim, okulum, ülkem. Some words also soften their last letter before a vowel: köpek becomes köpeğim, kitap becomes kitabım.

With a name, the owner gets an ending too, -in after a consonant and -nin after a vowel, with harmony: Zeynep'in annesi (Zeynep's mother), Mia'nın kedisi (Mia's cat). You can add benim (my) or senin (your) for stress, as in Tom benim arkadaşım, but the ending alone already carries the meaning.

examples.en: My mother and father are teachers.
Your sister is very kind.
Our dog is big and white.

body.en:
Turkish usually has no verb for 'to have'. Instead you say that your thing exists: kedim var, literally 'my cat exists', means 'I have a cat'. For 'I don't have', use yok: kedim yok. To ask, add mı: kedin var mı? (do you have a cat?)

After a number the noun stays singular: iki kedi (two cats), on dakika (ten minutes), never iki kediler. The same goes after kaç (how many): kaç tane kedin var?

For age, use yaşında, roughly 'at the age of': Deniz dokuz yaşında (Deniz is nine). Add -yım to talk about yourself: on iki yaşındayım (I am twelve).

examples.en: I have two sisters.
How many cats do you have?
I do not have a cat.

body.en:
For more than one thing, add -ler or -lar. Vowel harmony picks the ending: if the last vowel of the word is e, i, ö or ü, use -ler; if it is a, ı, o or u, use -lar. So domates becomes domatesler, muz becomes muzlar, elma becomes elmalar.

Leave the plural out after a number (üç patates, three potatoes) and when you speak about food in general: Ekmek ve peynir yerim, 'I eat bread and cheese'.

Use it for a group of things you can see or count: Muzlar sarı ve tatlı, 'the bananas are yellow and sweet'.

examples.en: The bananas are yellow and sweet.
The tomatoes are from our garden.
Ali eats fruit every day.

body.en:
Where English uses 'in', 'at' or 'on', Turkish adds -de or -da to the place: ev (house) becomes evde (at home), bahçe becomes bahçede (in the garden), oda becomes odada (in the room). Use -de after e, i, ö or ü, and -da after a, ı, o or u.

After a hard consonant (ç, f, h, k, p, s, ş, t) the d turns into t: mutfakta (in the kitchen), kitapta (in the book).

For 'on' and 'next to', Turkish uses place words with the same ending: masanın üstünde (on the table), kapının yanında (next to the door). Put var at the end to say that something is there: Mutfakta bir masa var, 'there is a table in the kitchen'.

examples.en: Emma is in the garden now.
My father cooks in the kitchen.
The book is on the bed.

body.en:
For habits and things that are generally true, Turkish uses the present with -r. Take the verb, drop -mek or -mak, and add -r with a vowel: yapmak becomes yapar (does), uyanmak becomes uyanır (wakes up), gitmek becomes gider (goes, the t softens to d). If the stem ends in a vowel, add just -r: okumak becomes okur (reads), uyumak becomes uyur (sleeps).

Then add the person: okurum (I read), okursun (you read), okur (he or she reads), okuruz (we read). The verb goes last, and a time word like her gün (every day) or sabahları (in the mornings) usually comes right after the person: Deniz her gün okula gider.

Short verbs usually take -er or -ar (içer, gider, yapar) and longer ones -ir, -ır, -ur or -ür (uyanır, çalışır). There are exceptions, like gelir (comes) and alır (takes), so learn each verb with its he or she form.

examples.en: I wake up at seven.
Deniz goes to school every day.
What do you do on the weekend?

body.en:
Two endings help you find the way. -e or -a means 'to': sola (to the left), parka (to the park), okula (to school). After a vowel a y joins: banka becomes bankaya.

-den or -dan means 'from': köşeden (from the corner), buradan (from here). After a hard consonant it turns into -ten or -tan: parktan (from the park). That is why Turkish says Köşeden sola dön, 'from the corner, turn to the left'.

Some words pick one of them. Yakın (near) takes 'to': Evim parka yakın, my house is near the park. Uzak (far) takes 'from': buradan uzak, far from here.

examples.en: Turn left at the corner.
My house is near the park.
Is the beach far from here?

title.en: The one I mean: the ending -i

body.en:
When the object of a verb is a specific thing, one you could point at, Turkish adds -i, -ı, -u or -ü to it: ceket (a jacket) becomes ceketi (the jacket). After a vowel a y joins: elbise becomes elbiseyi. Some words soften too: gömlek becomes gömleği.

Compare Mia siyah ayakkabı giyer (Mia wears black shoes, in general) with Kırmızı gömleği istiyorum (I want the red shirt, that one there).

When bu (this), şu or o (that) comes before the object, the thing is specific, so the ending is always there: Bu elbiseyi deneyebilir miyim? Can I try on this dress?

examples.en: I want the red shirt.
Can I try on this dress?
Mia wears black shoes.

body.en:
For something happening right now, Turkish uses -iyor. Drop -mek or -mak and add -iyor: yüzmek becomes yüzüyor (is swimming), kalmak becomes kalıyor (is staying). The first vowel follows harmony (-iyor, -ıyor, -uyor, -üyor), but -yor never changes.

If the stem ends in a vowel, add just -yor: okumak becomes okuyor. A final a or e turns into i, ı, u or ü: izlemek becomes izliyor.

Then add the person: kalıyorum (I am staying), kalıyorsun, kalıyor, kalıyoruz. For weather, Turkish says the rain or the snow is falling: yağmur yağıyor (it is raining), kar yağıyor (it is snowing).

examples.en: It is raining in Paris.
I am staying at home today.
Elif is reading on the beach.

title.en: It was: -di after nouns and adjectives

body.en:
To say 'was' or 'were', add -di to a noun or adjective. Harmony gives -di, -dı, -du or -dü: güzel becomes güzeldi (was beautiful), yorgun becomes yorgundu (was tired). After a vowel a y joins: harika becomes harikaydı.

After a hard consonant the d turns into t: yavaş becomes yavaştı (was slow), uzak becomes uzaktı (was far).

Add the person at the end: yorgundum (I was tired), yorgundun (you were), yorgundu (he or she was), yorgunduk (we were). It works with places too: trendeydik, 'we were on the train'. For 'was not', use değildi: Biletler pahalı değildi.

examples.en: The bus was very slow.
We were on the train at six.
Was the bed comfortable?

body.en:
The same -di ending makes the past of verbs. Drop -mek or -mak and add -di: görmek becomes gördü (saw), aramak becomes aradı (called), bulmak becomes buldu (found). After a hard consonant the d turns into t: unutmak becomes unuttu (forgot), dans etmek becomes dans etti (danced).

The person endings are short: gördüm (I saw), gördün (you saw), gördü (he or she saw), gördük (we saw), gördüler (they saw). Time words like dün (yesterday) usually come early, right after the person: Emma dün beni aradı.

Use this past for things you saw or did yourself. It is the one for telling a friend about your weekend: Emre ile buluştuk, sonra dans ettik.

examples.en: I saw Elif yesterday.
We danced at the party.
Elif forgot her bag at school.

body.en:
To talk about plans, add -ecek or -acak to the verb stem: gelmek becomes gelecek (will come), yapmak becomes yapacak (will do or make). After a vowel a y joins: aramak becomes arayacak (will call).

Before a vowel the k softens to ğ: arayacağım (I will call), arayacaksın (you will call), arayacak (he or she will call), arayacağız (we will call). The t of etmek and gitmek softens to d: ziyaret edeceğim (I will visit), gideceğiz (we will go). Gelecek also means 'next': gelecek hafta, next week.

To invite a friend, put ister misin? (would you like?) after a verb in -mek or -mak: Bizimle gelmek ister misin? A warm yes is Çok isterim! or Tabii ki!

examples.en: I am going to call you tomorrow.
Mia is going to cook tonight.
Would you like to come with us?
